headline: Maryland residents urged to conserve water after storm disrupts power
author: Tim Craig, Liam Scott

paragraphs.text: Nearly 2 million people in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties in Maryland were asked to conserve water on Thanksgiving after a major storm disrupted power supplies at two water-filtration plants.
In a news release Thursday afternoon, the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC) said it was issuing the alert “out of an abundance of caution” due to “intermittent power disruptions.”
Residents were asked to utilize “only water that is necessary” and limit showers, toilet flushing, and the use of washing machines and dishwashers.
“Following the guidance … could help preserve water for system storage and fire protection until the storm passes and power reliability is restored,” WSSC Water said.

WSSC Water’s Potomac plant, which is the larger of the two facilities and provides drinking water to about 75 percent of the region’s 1.9 million customers, had power and was producing drinking water as of around 4 p.m., according to spokesman Chuck Brown.
The problem, Brown said, is that the facility has experienced several power disruptions due to the storm.

WSSC Water’s other water-filtration plant, Patuxent, is out of service for planned maintenance, according to Brown, but crews are working to bring it back online. That facility also was experiencing power disruptions due to the storm, he said.
The agency stressed that the water remains safe to drink and cook with, and that there is no need for it to be boiled.
“This is a rapidly evolving situation, and WSSC Water will provide continuous updates to keep customers informed,” the agency said.
WSSC Water spokesman Luis Maya said the agency didn’t have an estimate on how long the conservation alert would stay in place. He said that would depend on how long the storm lasts.
“We’re hoping on the shorter end. At the end of the storm, we’ll have a better idea,” he said. “We want to make sure we’re prepared in case this is a prolonged event.”
Once power is stable again, Maya said the agency will lift the alert and notify residents that they can go back to normal water usage.

The conservation alert comes as wind gusts exceeding 60 mph rocked the Washington region Thursday. Pepco, the electric utility in suburban Maryland, reports nearly 25,000 customers had lost power as of 3 p.m.
